scenes.narration: The Dark Tower: The Gunslinger did not evolve to be understood — only to be survived. The Dark Tower: The Gunslinger is a dark-fantasy novel by American author Stephen King. The Gunslinger was first published in 1982 as a fix-up novel, joining five short stories that had been published between 1978 and 1981.

The honest version of The Dark Tower: The Gunslinger starts by giving up the comforting part. King substantially revised the novel in 2003; this version has remained in print ever since, with the subtitle "RESUMPTION". The story centers on Roland Deschain, the last gunslinger, who has been chasing his adversary, "the man in black," for many years.

Strip The Dark Tower: The Gunslinger of its poetry and the mechanism underneath is stranger. The novel fuses Western fiction with fantasy, science fiction, and horror, following Roland's trek through a vast desert and beyond in search of the man in black. Roland meets several people along his journey, including a boy named Jake, who travels with him part of the way.

Evolution does not optimize for happiness — The Dark Tower: The Gunslinger shows exactly where that breaks. The novel was inspired by Robert Browning's poem "Childe Roland to the Dark Tower Came" (1855), which King read as a sophomore at the University of Maine. King explains that he "played with the idea of trying a long romantic novel embodying the feel, if not the exact sense, of the Browning poem." King started writing this novel in 1970 on a ream of bright green paper that he found at the library.

What looks like free choice in The Dark Tower: The Gunslinger is older than choice itself. The following year, because the Pet Sematary cover noted The Gunslinger among King's previous works, many fans called the offices of King, Grant, and Doubleday wanting more information on the already-out-of-print book. In 2003, the novel was reissued in a revised and expanded version with modified language and added and changed scenes intended to resolve inconsistencies with the later books in the series.

Nobody designed the part of The Dark Tower: The Gunslinger you experience — it was inherited. The book tells the story of The Gunslinger, Roland of Gilead, and his quest to catch the man in black, the first of many steps toward Roland's ultimate destination, The Dark Tower. The main story takes place in a world somewhat similar to the Old West but in an alternate timeframe or parallel universe.

Every serious account of The Dark Tower: The Gunslinger eventually collides with the question of who is deciding. As Roland travels across the desert in search of the man in black, whom he knows as Walter, he encounters a farmer named Brown and his raven, Zoltan. Roland spends the night there and recalls his time spent in Tull, a small town Roland passed through not long before meeting them.

Nihilism is not the conclusion of The Dark Tower: The Gunslinger — it is the floor you stand on while examining it. The man in black had also stayed in the town; he brought a dead man stricken by addiction to the opiate-like "devil grass" back to life and left a trap for Roland. Roland meets the leader of the local church, who reveals to him that the man in black impregnated her with a demon.

The selfish-gene reading of The Dark Tower: The Gunslinger makes it less romantic and far more precise. When he awakens the morning after telling Brown the story, his mule is dead, forcing him to continue on foot. Roland arrives at an abandoned way station and first encounters Jake Chambers, a young boy.

Freud is not dead; he is simply no longer allowed to be the whole answer. Jake remembers neither how long he has been at the way station nor exactly how he got there, and he hid when the man in black passed through. Roland hypnotizes Jake to determine the details of where he came from and discovers he died in a different universe that appears much closer in nature to our own.

The feeling that The Dark Tower: The Gunslinger means something is a chemical event with an evolutionary address. Before they leave, Roland and Jake search for food in a cellar and encounter a demon, which uses a skeleton entombed behind a wall to speak to them. Roland rescues Jake from an encounter with a succubus and gives him the jawbone to use as a protective charm against it.

Nothing in The Dark Tower: The Gunslinger was built for you — it was built for reproduction. Roland leaves him at camp and couples with the succubus, who is also an oracle, to learn more about his fate and the path to the Dark Tower. In a flashback, it is revealed that Roland is the son of Steven Deschain, a Gunslinger and lord of Gilead.

The psychology underneath The Dark Tower: The Gunslinger is simpler and older than the story on top. Roland was tricked into a premature test of manhood by dueling with Cort at age 14, earlier than any other apprentice. Roland defeated Cort in battle by choosing his hawk, David, as his weapon and sacrificing him to distract Cort.

Behind The Dark Tower: The Gunslinger sits an animal brain negotiating with a story it tells itself. He says that only he and Roland will meet on the other side, exacerbating Jake's fears that Roland will either kill or abandon him. Roland and Jake make their way into twisting tunnels within the mountain, traveling on an old railway handcar.

The nihilist does not deny The Dark Tower: The Gunslinger — he only refuses to flatter it. They are attacked by subterranean creatures called "Slow Mutants." At the tunnel's exit, they continue on foot. As the track on which they are traveling begins to break, Roland lets Jake fall into an abyss and continues his quest.

What culture calls destiny in The Dark Tower: The Gunslinger is usually just selection pressure wearing a suit. After sacrificing Jake in the mountain, Roland makes his way down to speak with the man in black. The man in black reads Roland's fate from a pack of cards that includes omens such as "the sailor," "the prisoner," "the lady of shadows," "death," and the Tower itself.

The genes do not care about The Dark Tower: The Gunslinger; they care about copies. The man in black states that he is a pawn of Roland's true enemy, who now controls the Dark Tower itself. Roland refuses, and the man in black tells him to go west before putting him to sleep.

Take away the meaning and The Dark Tower: The Gunslinger still functions — that is the disturbing part. When Roland awakens, 10 years have passed, and there is a skeleton next to him that he assumes to be the man in black. Roland takes the jawbone from the skeleton, as a replacement for the one he gave to Jake, before traveling to the shore of the Western Sea.

The unconscious does not argue with The Dark Tower: The Gunslinger; it simply acts first. In his introduction to the new edition, King stated that he felt the original version was "dry" and difficult for new readers to access. He also made the storytelling more linear and the book's plot more consistent with the series ending.

The Dark Tower: The Gunslinger feels chosen. The evidence says it was installed. Other changes were made to resolve continuity errors introduced by later volumes. Later information presented in The Drawing of the Three suggests paper is a scarcity in Roland's world.

The bleak reading of The Dark Tower: The Gunslinger is also the most testable one. Reference to 12 years having passed since the fall of Gilead, which happened when Roland was a teenager, is changed to "unknown years." Otherwise, it would be deduced that Roland is in his 30s, whereas later books imply Roland is ancient. Likewise, the man in black originally says he is "nearly immortal;" in the revision, he says this of both himself and Roland.

Modern psychology keeps rediscovering what the pessimists said first about The Dark Tower: The Gunslinger. Roland's cold-hearted killing of Allie is changed to make him appear more humane. Originally, when the town of Tull turns on Roland, Allie is seized by a townsperson and used as a human shield.

The self that experiences The Dark Tower: The Gunslinger is a committee, not a king. In the revised version, she has been driven mad by Walter by the time she is seized, and she begs Roland to put her out of her misery. References to the Beast were changed to refer to the Crimson King, who otherwise is not mentioned in the series until The Waste Lands.

Reproduction explains more of The Dark Tower: The Gunslinger than any philosophy dares to admit. The Taheen are a race of creatures that wouldn't originally appear until the final three books. A major textual change is the fate and identity of the man in black.

Once you see The Dark Tower: The Gunslinger as an adaptation, the mystery mostly evaporates. In the original text, Walter's death at the end of the story is of no uncertainty to Roland. In the revised edition, Roland speculates whether his discovery of Walter's bones is some trick or whether Walter has truly died.

The story The Dark Tower: The Gunslinger tells about itself is the last thing to be trusted. Even after the death of Walter, Broadcloak was still to be found and killed. Later, in Wizard and Glass, Walter and Marten, along with Randall Flagg, are all revealed to be the same person.

Meaning is not found in The Dark Tower: The Gunslinger — it is manufactured for it. Although no reference to the name "Flagg" is made in the revised edition of The Gunslinger, all references to Walter and Marten are altered so that it is plausible they are the same man. In general, the world the gunslinger walked through in the original text was a run-down version of our own.

The cold light on The Dark Tower: The Gunslinger leaves the facts intact and only the comfort removed. The text mentions England, the star Polaris, Mars, Jesus and other biblical figures, Easter, All-Saint's Eve (Halloween), and Greek and Egyptian gods. In the revision, most of these references were removed to make Roland's world only vaguely like ours.
